extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, judges, and advanced students of patent law
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for construing patent specifications and claims, allocating questions of law and fact between court and jury, and the types and use of evidence in patent litigation (title, novelty, sufficiency, infringement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court may consider evidence of the actual invention and state of the art when construing claims
rubrics_metrics.description: In the progress of a trial the state of the art, the surrounding circumstances in which the inventor was placed, the previous existence of some things mentioned or referred to in the patent, will all be likely to be developed on the evidence; and these facts may materially affect the construction to be given to the claim. The judge must gather as he goes along; informing himself upon the evidence, and observing what facts are controverted, and what facts are not controverted, which bear upon the meaning of the claim, in reference to its extent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If facts material to construction are not left in doubt on the evidence, the construction will be given to the jury absolutely; but if the evidence requires a finding of facts by the jury, the construction will be given to them conditionally. The court should receive and watch evidence and apply it to construction, but must take care that evidence is not allowed to supply positive omissions which would render the specification defective. (§§457, 463)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior existence of matter mentioned affects extent of claim; patentee presumed not to claim things known in use
rubrics_metrics.description: If it is manifest, on the face of the terms in which the patentee has described his invention, that he has included something of which he was not the inventor, his patent cannot be allowed to cover it. The degree or extent to which that thing was known before, its great familiarity and constant use for analogous purposes, will be important elements in the question whether the patentee has claimed it as of his own invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This consideration supports the rule that the patentee is to be presumed not to intend to claim things which he must know to be in use; specifications should be read so, consistently with the fair import of language, as to make the claim coextensive with the actual discovery or invention. (§§458–459)

rubrics_metrics.name: State of the art limits interpretation of broad/generic terms (ejusdem generis principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a patent contemplates the use of certain substances, although it may use terms extensive enough to embrace other substances ascertained later to be capable of the same use, the general terms will be interpreted to include only those substances ejusdem generis with the particular substances mentioned which may reasonably be supposed, on the state of the art, to have been contemplated at the time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether particular later-discovered substances fall within the general terms is a matter to be ascertained by evidence and depends on what would reasonably have been contemplated given the state of the art when the patent issued. (§459–460; example of gas apparatus and oil)

rubrics_metrics.name: Facts expressly or implicitly referred to in the specification form part of the description and may govern construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes the construction may rest on facts which are so referred to as to make a part of the description and to govern it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If these facts are controverted they are to be left to the jury; but if they are proved or admitted, the court will take notice of them in giving a legal construction to the instrument. (Illustrated by speeder/bow-flier example). (§461)

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of the description (enablement) is a question of fact for the jury
rubrics_metrics.description: The sufficiency of the description to enable competent persons to apply the invention is a question of fact for the jury, to be determined upon the testimony of experts and the language itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The jury determines whether the directions are sufficiently clear and explicit to enable a competent workman to practise the invention; however, the information of what the specification has said is to come from the court. If the specification requires a workman to ascertain by experiment the exact proportions (i.e., undue experimentation), the court must pronounce the patent invalid. (§462)

rubrics_metrics.name: Court declares the meaning of the specification; jury decides factual sufficiency and meanings of words of art when evidence is required
rubrics_metrics.description: The meaning of the specification is for the court to declare; the jury's province is, after being informed what the specification has said, to determine whether the directions are sufficient to enable a competent workman to practise the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When words of art or surrounding circumstances affect meaning, the court may instruct the jury that the specification has said so and so, according as they find the meaning of the scientific terms or circumstances. If there are no words of art and no surrounding circumstances to be ascertained, the court will instruct the jury what the specification has said and then the jury will determine sufficiency. (§§462–464; Neilson v. Harford discussion)

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between questions of law and fact: patentable subject matter is for the court
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the invention disclosed by the specification is a proper subject for a patent is a question of law, on which the court will instruct the jury. It may involve many facts, but when those facts are ascertained it is purely a legal question whether the invention is a patentable subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is distinct from novelty (a question of fact). The court decides whether the alleged invention falls within classes of discoveries recognized by patent law; e.g., mere application of an old thing to a new purpose may not be patentable, while a known thing used in a known manner to produce economically beneficial results may be. (§468)

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty is a prerequisite and is a question of fact
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelty of the invention is a prerequisite to validity of the patent and is a question of fact to be determined from the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the claimed thing is new, the court must decide whether it is the kind of invention the law recognizes as patentable (see also §468).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement is a question of fact as to substantial identity
rubrics_metrics.description: The question of infringement is whether the invention of the defendant is substantially the same thing as that of the plaintiff. The identity of two things is a matter of fact, depending upon evidence, and is to be determined by the jury under proper instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This holds even where the defendant's process or machine is undisputed; the court cannot itself compare and declare identity — the jury must find facts establishing substantial sameness. (Reference to chemical equivalents issues in Heath's patent). (§469)

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant's status as licensee under another patent is not a defense to infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: On the question of infringement, it is no answer for the defendant to show that he is a licensee under another patent and that his machine is made in accordance with that patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being licensed under a different patent does not avoid liability for infringing the plaintiff's patent. (§469a)

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence in patent causes divides into evidence of title and evidence of infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The evidence appropriate to the different stages of a patent cause may be divided into (1) the evidence of title, and (2) the evidence upon the point of infringement. Evidence of title relates to the letters-patent and the plaintiff's interest therein, the novelty and utility of the invention, and the sufficiency of the specification. Evidence of the infringement relates to the identity of the thing made, used, or practised by the defendant, with the invention of the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a basic evidentiary classification to guide presentation and proof at trial. (§470)

rubrics_metrics.name: Certified copy of letters-patent is competent evidence of grant; related patents may need to be produced
rubrics_metrics.description: A copy of the letters-patent under the seal of the Patent Office and the signature of the commissioner is competent evidence that a patent has been granted for the invention described in the specification annexed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patent produced in evidence refers to the description in a former patent, it is necessary to produce and read that former patent to show what the invention is if it is not made entirely clear by the patent on which the action is brought. (§471)

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner's reissue decision is conclusive on inadvertence/mistake except for fraud or lack of jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the patentee has surrendered his original patent and taken out a reissue with an amended specification, the action of the commissioner of patents in granting the reissue is conclusive evidence upon the question of 'inadvertence, accident, or mistake.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision of the commissioner is not re-examinable elsewhere except upon the ground of fraud or evident want of jurisdiction. (Stimpson v. Westchester Railroad). (§471a)

rubrics_metrics.name: Specifications should be construed liberally to sustain inventors when practicable
rubrics_metrics.description: A liberal construction is to be given to a patent, and inventors sustained, if practicable, without a departure from sound principles. Only thus can ingenuity and perseverance be encouraged to advance the arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should sustain specifications if they can fairly, not be astute to avoid inventions; but this liberal construction must not conflict with other settled principles (e.g., reasonable certainty of description). (Citations: Grant v. Raymond, Russell v. Cowley, Wyeth v. Stone). (§462 note)

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of scientific words and surrounding circumstances may require evidence to ascertain; court cannot judicially notice them without evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The court has no judicial knowledge of the terms of art or the surrounding circumstances and cannot say until it has heard the evidence that the meaning is not to be affected by them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore the plaintiff is always entitled to offer evidence to show that the specification's meaning is affected by such words or circumstances; the court must receive and watch the evidence and determine limits. (§463)

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction must not be drawn into the province of the jury; separate intelligibility (enablement) from construction
rubrics_metrics.description: The provinces of the court and the jury are distinct: while the jury decides whether the specification sufficiently describes the mode of carrying the invention into effect, the meaning of the very passages on which this question arises, in relation to the prior question of what the specification has said, is for the court after the facts have been ascertained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Care must be taken to separate the question of intelligibility (jury) from the question of construction/meaning (court); they may arise from the same passages but are always separable. (§464)

rubrics_metrics.name: If specification on its face shows inclusion of known matter, patent cannot cover that matter
rubrics_metrics.description: If it is manifest on the face of the specification that the patentee has included something of which he was not the inventor, his patent cannot be allowed to cover it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where it is doubtful whether he has so included it, the extent to which that thing was known and in use will be important in deciding whether he intended to claim it. This supports presumption against claiming known public matter. (§458)
